Hi Team, we've completed the *preliminary calculations* of driver coverage, detailed in the [*10 Feb 2025 - Exploration Results*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1RTin2gd28-L_lYSJJEwnfVn-7ZzvKxm73iQxaAdvVL0/edit?tab=t.442fordr28sg#heading=h.s44zny14axla] section.

*Method:*
We proceed with Calculation Option 2 (Total Addressable Users = New Entry + Carried-Over):

* *New Entry:* Users who joined this lifecycle stage in *January 2025*.
* *Carried-Over:* Users who remained in the same stage from *previous months* without progressing.

*Coverage Observations*:
After applying the agreed calculation, we identified that *percentage coverage remains low across all lifecycle stages (≤10%), except for retention.*
However, when we *separate New Entry vs. Carried-Over*, we see that *Carried-Over users significantly impact the overall coverage, dragging the percentage down*
For example for leads stage:

* *Leads (Overall) Coverage = 10%*
* *Leads Coverage - New Entry = 83%*
* *Leads Coverage - Carried-Over = 6%*

For Carried-Over leads, we further analyzed their tenure and lead application status:

* 89% of Carried-Over users are in the "In Progress" status
* Among these users, *_64.15% registered before 2024,_* while 24.75% registered in 2024.
* _Question: Should we define addressable users based on the past XX months to exclude users who are no longer approachable?_


Although New Entry leads coverage is better (83%), it is still below the expected 95% (since we expect every registered lead to receive at least 1 email)

* Notably, Portugal, Greece, and Mexico have particularly low coverage (≤30%), prompting further investigation into potential communication gaps in these markets.
* _Question: Are we intentionally not prioritizing communications for these countries, or is this an unexpected gap?_

Hi [~accountid:712020:85a31a38-edb2-4253-b037-fa5bcad14728] - This has been already sent out last week. Counterparty has signed as well, still waiting for Nikolai to sign, but he is currently on a vacation.

*Checking if the rest of the effect is related to priors.*

There’re are now only two changes that we do Q over Q to the models - changing the period and the priors.

In the previous comment we have shown that additional data only has the impact on coefficients when new data brings new signal (and this is what we want from the model).

Now, it means that the rest of the changes in coefficients should come from changes in priors.  Below we give more details on how it worked out for some markets.

*Stockholm*

* Original Q3 model had very informed priors for iOS keeping the coefficients quite high, like {{{'vmax': {'mu':282, 'sigma':10}}}} (see [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359379093?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359379117])
* Q4 models set the priors to be less informed (with {{sigma=66}} almost for all channels) - see [this|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1cL6Ur8uJh5oA-DFlrSGYpGsNPc18yik81vORRcSj6Pw/edit?pli=1&gid=0#gid=0] copy from original output (or similarly this [file|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IMLDCHtWVpbUWx4xWuWBk7iYFsnUvkCkW3gso5ui4-U/edit?gid=1612750349#gid=1612750349])
* Running the models with weaker priors in Q3 would give the same result as in Q4 (i.e. we’ve bee keeping up good coefficients with priors exclusively) - see [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359379976?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359380002]
** Interestingly, making the prior less informed did not change the situation for {{Google Android}} (vmax=36 vs vmax=41), meaning that priors did not play a huge role there.

*Paris*

* Original Q3 models for Paris all had the priors with {{sigma=50}}
* Having those same priors, but less informed ({{sigma=100}}) would:
** not really change Google Android {{vmax=354}} to {{vmax=359}}
** change vmax for all iOS channels by ~ 30% (from 300-ish to 200-ish)
** (Meaning that assessment of iOS performance could actually be a bit inflated)
* While modelling Q4, *vmax priors were also decreased* (which also contributed to us having lower coefficients):
** Google Android: 365 →  9 (probably under the influence of expiment)
** Google iOS 477 → 318
** Tiktok iOS 450 → 424
** Snapchat 93 → 44

*Berlin*

*Priors* in Berlin for Q4 models were also generally *decreased* (comparing [this|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/3292131742150652?o=3829506390716583#command/3292131742150678] notebook to results from spreadsheet, like in Paris):

* Google Android: 260 → 8
* Facebook Android: 170 →  182
* Tiktok Android: 187 → 39
* Google iOS: 287 → 94
* Facebook iOS:  172 → 109 
* Tiktok iOS:  565 → 440
* Snapchat iOS:  55 → 40

Running the Q3 notebook for Berlin with larger sigmas also generally led to decrease of vmax except 

* faceboook android (which actually increased)
* tiktok ios (which stayed almost the same)



This should be a signal for us to be more attentive on how we define prior sigmas (and how informed we want our priors to be).

For example, most of the priors for Germany were from {{#past model}}. Should we be using past model’s indication with some increased sigmas?

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Requestor is from the ‘AI for CS’ team.
* Currently, several issues escalated by users are limited to a single interaction with AI, so that safety cases do not get lost with AI stopping the user from speaking to a person. Issue here, however, is that some issues are resolved quicker with AI, so automatic human escalation creates delays.
* As a result, new UK feature ‘Escalation on Demand’ will allow the user to +_choose_+ to contact a human after a specific number of interactions.
** For the issue cases flagged in the description, these are limited to 1 interaction.
** For critical safety cases, these will still be escalated to a human automatically, and will be unaffected by this feature (see [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C02N479PM9T/p1738341470394519?thread_ts=1738148277.300709&cid=C02N479PM9T]).
** If rider accidentally selects AI, they would still be escalated automatically to a human after two more interactions with AI.
* *Request for Privacy:* Are we ok with replacing the current hard escalation (i.e., always escalating to a human after one interaction with AI) to showing ‘Escalation on Demand’ after one interaction?

+*ANALYSIS*+

* We are not processing any new data per se, nor are we introducing any new form of AI. We are just giving users the option (for certain cases) to more actively choose whether they want to deal with AI or a person to handle their case. Primarily a *process change*.
** Similarly, does not directly relate to issues in the ICO / AKI investigations.
* Risk profile = Low. *Seems fine to green-light*.

Hi [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a], 

To summarise the process a bit better than AI:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
# *Duplicate E-mail/phone number/IBAN/Driver’s License*

* DL reaches out to Bolt CS on why they cannot register with their details
* We check for the duplicate Driver profile
** Based on the duplicate type, there’s a different way to find the duplicate Driver profile

# *CS performs account checks*
## Check if the duplicate Driver has verified themselves, in Admin
## Check IBAN account owner by performing a dummy money transfer
## Check if IBAN has received payouts in Admin
## *IF duplicate driver’s license*, we will *ALSO* ask the DL to come in for a DEC visit, so we can verify their driver’s license against a local regulatory database (in case for GH, it would be the DVLA). We will also check the duplicate Driver driver’s license against the database. 
# *Determine account ownership*
## *We can assume the duplicate driver has committed identity fraud, if we can find combination of inconsistencies in the existing account:* 
### ED failed verification, verification not taken, or false positive
### Driver Licence on existing account looks edited
### Driver Licence information on regulator portal matches DL ID
### IBAN registered in DL's name (and no payouts received = stronger suspicion)
## *We can assume the DL is aware of an already existing account or uses already existing details, if:*
### The current active driver passed verification
### IBAN belongs to current active driver 
### Current active driver’s Driver Licence verified with Local Authority, DL did not pass same verification
### *We can assume DL is aware of the account if*: 
### Driver verification shows DL’s face 
### DL and current driver’s info and docs match one another 
### IBAN belongs to DL and has received payouts
# *If we determined that DL is aware of the already existing account, or tries to register with another driver’s details*
## CS will advise accordingly (Advise DL to register with valid docs/details, log into their already existin account)
# *If we determined that the duplicate driver likely has committed identity fraud*
## We inform the DL that their application is on hold for further verification
## Suspend the current active driver, inform them of account suspension and ask them to come in a DEC visit for physical verification
### If current driver refuses or doesn’t respond, CS escalates the case to Local OPS who will delete the account, DL can than register again
### If current driver also passes physical verification, we will either ask both parties to use separate e-mail/phone number, or to resolve the data conflict with the local regulatory body (DVLA for GH)
### If current driver doesn’t pass physical verification:
#### *Duplicate driver’s license:* CS escalates the case to Local OPS who will delete the account, DL can than register again
#### *Duplicate e-mail, phone number, IBAN:* 
##### If current driver still denies fraud they will remain suspended and we will change their account details so DL can register again
##### If current driver admits fraud they will regain access to the account, we will change the account details so DL can register again. 
{panel}

# Currently, this process would only work in GH since this process requires a DEC visit. The reason for that is that we cannot process documents in Beehive tickets, e.g. a photo from a user holding a driver’s license next to their face. Correct me if I’m wrong [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a]. I read that that is not compliant, since this is sensitive information, and cannot be stored on BH. 
# Correct, i’m also concerned about how we communicate it. 
## At no point will we communicate what field flagged as a duplicate to DL (e.g. duplicate e-mail). 
## If we need the DL to come in for a DEC visit, CS can state it’s for *verification purposes*. At the DEC visit, CS can state that they have encountered some challenges verifying some of the details of the application. If the case is particularly complex, we can also ask the DL to leave the DEC because we need additional time. 
## If we determined ID fraud, we will let the current driver know his account is suspended due to strong suspicion of fraudulent activity. 
## We can indeed assure the DL that we take this seriously, that we took appropriate actions to the current driver (I don’t think we can say that we suspend the current driver??), and that we can cooperate with Law Enforcement if the DL so wishes to lodge a fraud case with the local police. But we can only say that if the DL knows there’s duplicate data in our database, the first thing we communicate is that there are verification issues.

Hi [~accountid:712020:c0f6fbe7-f5ae-44e2-bb6c-8e5815ace0d9] , adding my comments from a privacy POV:

We only have one clause governing data protection/privacy, and it only states:

* Each party processes personal data independently, meaning both parties are Data Controllers. Each is responsible for determining the purposes and means of their own data processing and must ensure compliance with applicable data protection laws (e.g., GDPR).
* This means that each party bears its own risk related to personal data processing. If one party experiences a data breach or GDPR non-compliance, only that party is liable, not the other.

*Summary:* This setup is aligned with our general approach, ensuring we maintain control over our data processing activities. It’s favorable compared to other tenders where we operated under the municipality’s instructions, as this gives us more autonomy and clarity on our responsibilities.

h4. *Some key risks:*

# *No specific liability cap for privacy law violations:*
## It means that GDPR fines or damages related to data breaches will fall under the overall liability provisions in the agreement.
## If we incur a fine or experience a breach due to our fault or the fault of our service providers (e.g., customer support), we will be fully liable.
# There is no mention of cooperation for handling *Data Subject Access Requests (DSARs*), which could lead to inconsistent responses and potential non-compliance. Low risk. If they receive requests - they respond to them; we will do the same.
# The absence of a clause requiring mutual notification/cooperation in case of a *data breach* could result in delayed reporting or lack of support during investigations.
# No provisions regarding international data transfers, which could lead to compliance gaps if data is transferred outside the EEA. I then assume there will be no transfers outside the EU/EEA.



*What we’ll need to do is* develop clear communications for drivers, covering data collected through alcolocs/name tags and their rights, as far as that relates to sharing their personal data (i.e. displaying it in the cars to other passengers). I suggest this to be done *not* via a privacy notice, but as a separate notification, to make sure that we target these specific drivers, and not all drivers in Sweden.

This is a translation, so we’ll adjust it accordingly if we have a final version of the agreement.

* We don’t have any standard clauses for KPIs for body and engineering works, but this can be integrated. Usually it’s integrated under the pricing annex. KPIs are good for standardized processes. One way would be to agree some standard works that have time- and monetary limit. Essentially - if you have some source materials what you’ll be asking from the firms I can adjust it accordingly. 
* If you do have some indications of the limits applicable to the supplier for specific works, it would be wise to integrate them to the price list. 
* We can agree -for example- that they should be ready to take in our vehicle in X hours or days. If they breach the KPI, then we can apply contractual penalty of 5/10% of the cost of the works. As the conditions can differ by the workshops, it would be reasonable to integrate these terms to the price list or special terms.
* Warranty conditions can be either agreed in the agreement or in the offer. If you have a standard set of warranty conditions, then let’s integrate it. Warranty can be anything and there isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution here. We can set the warranty period as time (6 months). We can set it as mileage (10 000 km). We can set it as maintenance interval (6 months or 15 000 km, whichever is longer). We can set it as lifetime of the replacement part. Essentially - a commercial term and this will be reflected on the price.
* As an exception, we could set a firm limit to body (paint) jobs - that all the works done must correspond to the manufacturer’s standards and they should give a warranty at least 12 months. Any defect discovered during that time will be rectified without any additional costs. There is always a but - this warranty can be only given if the works are done properly by the SOP. If we give instructions not to follow the SOP, then warranty is also not applicable.

*Business decision needed to limit refund periods per vertical*

Commerce Legal provides guidance on payment processes for customers and partners, including related functionalities such as Bolt Balance, billing, and fiscalization.

The issue of refunds is closely tied to service provision, as a user’s entitlement to a refund depends directly on the nature of the service. Refunds generally fall into two categories:

*Type 1 – True Refunds:* Legally mandated refunds that users are entitled to.

*Type 2 – Compensational Refunds:* Voluntary refunds issued by Bolt despite no legal obligation.

*The business aims to limit the timeframe for refund requests to make the process more manageable.* +*Since refund periods impact the user experience, any decision to impose restrictions must carefully balance business needs with potential legal risks.*+



To support decision-making, vertical leads require legal guidance on:

* The statutory limitation period applicable to refunds (assumed to apply only to Type 1 refunds).
* Risks associated with implementing a shorter refund period, including potential consumer complaints.

If a decision is made to restrict the refund period, the Terms & Conditions will need to be updated accordingly.

Just FYI, in summer 2024 Commerce Legal intern Yagmur Atilgan conducted a [+comparative analysis of refund policies between Bolt and Uber+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1F5END_8tGwcTWhSDvtRdajEmsYIdOWZ9CdBCjdvyDXk/edit?usp=sharing]. *Prompt:* What a carsharing company should consider, mainly from Privacy and Legal angles, in order to implement an automated exchange of users' blacklists with a competitor in Germany?

*Output:* 

*1. Data Protection & Privacy (GDPR)*

Since blacklists likely contain personal data (e.g., names, contact details, reasons for blacklisting), the *General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)* applies. Key considerations include:

h4. *a) Legal Basis for Data Sharing (Art. 6 GDPR)*

* *Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f))*: The company may argue a legitimate interest in preventing fraud, misconduct, or safety risks. However, this requires a balancing test to ensure users' rights are not disproportionately affected.
* *Consent (Art. 6(1)(a))*: Getting users’ explicit consent would be the safest route but is impractical due to high opt-out rates.
* *Legal Obligation (Art. 6(1)(c))*: Only applicable if a law explicitly requires such a blacklist exchange (which is unlikely in this case).

h4. *b) Necessity & Proportionality (Data Minimization, Art. 5(1)(c))*

* Data must be *limited* to what is strictly necessary (e.g., reasons for blacklisting must be objectively justified and limited to serious breaches like fraud or violence).
* *Timeframe for retention* should be clearly defined.

h4. *c) Transparency (Art. 13 & 14 GDPR)*

* *Privacy Policies & Notices:* Users must be informed that their data could be shared with competitors.
* *Right to Object (Art. 21 GDPR):* Users have the right to contest their blacklisting and the sharing of their data.

h4. *d) Special Categories of Data (Art. 9 GDPR)*

* If blacklists include *criminal records, health-related incidents, or racial/religious markers*, additional safeguards apply.
* Data *must not be discriminatory* (e.g., banning users based on nationality or disability).

h4. *e) Data Subject Rights*

* Users have *the right to access, rectify, and erase their data* under GDPR.
* A *clear dispute resolution mechanism* must be in place to correct false or unjustified blacklisting.

----

h3. *2. Antitrust Considerations*

Data-sharing between competitors raises *competition law risks*, particularly under German and EU law:

h4. *a) Collusion & Market Impact*

* Sharing blacklist data might *reduce competition* if it results in an *industry-wide ban* for certain customers.
* The *Bundeskartellamt (Federal Cartel Office)* could view this as an *anti-competitive agreement* if it limits users’ ability to switch services.

h4. *b) Justification under Competition Law*

To be legally defensible, the blacklist exchange must:

* *Demonstrate necessity* (e.g., safety concerns, fraud prevention).
* *Ensure fairness & non-discrimination* (i.e., objective criteria for blacklisting).
* *Have independent oversight* (e.g., third-party arbiter or regulatory approval).

----

h3. *3. Technical & Security Compliance*

The exchange system must comply with *IT security and data transfer* requirements:

h4. *a) Data Sharing Infrastructure*

* Use *secure APIs or encrypted channels* for data transfer.
* Consider *pseudonymization* or *hashing* to reduce privacy risks.

h4. *b) Data Processing Agreements (DPAs)*

If a third-party service is involved, a *Data Processing Agreement (Art. 28 GDPR)* is required.

h4. *c) Logging & Auditing*

* Maintain *records of blacklisted users and reasons*.
* Implement *internal compliance checks* to avoid wrongful blacklisting.

----

h3. *4. Regulatory & Industry Guidelines*

* *Bundeskartellamt* (Federal Cartel Office) guidance on data-sharing.
* *Data Protection Authorities (DPA)* in Germany (BfDI or local state DPAs) should be consulted.
* *Industry Codes of Conduct* (if applicable) could help reduce legal risks.

----

h3. *5. Alternative Approaches to Reduce Risk*

* *Industry-wide fraud prevention database* governed by a neutral entity.
* *Anonymous risk scoring models* instead of explicit blacklisting.
* *Limited data sharing* (e.g., only sharing hashed identifiers of high-risk users).

----

h3. *Conclusion*

A direct automated blacklist exchange with competitors *carries high GDPR and antitrust risks*. To proceed: ✅ *Justify data-sharing under GDPR (Legitimate Interest)* ✅ *Limit scope & retention period* ✅ *Ensure transparency & user rights* ✅ *Assess competition law risks* ✅ *Use secure & audited data-sharing mechanisms*

*Valid legal basis:* The Art. 219 Transmission of personal data

 (1) A state or local government authority, health care provider or *other third party shall transmit* +*without the consent of the data subject,*+ *at the request of an insurance undertaking, personal data or grant access thereto if the personal data are necessary to the insurance undertaking for the performance of an insurance contract and ensuring the performance thereof or for exercising the right of recourse.* The transmission of personal data to the insurance undertaking or granting access thereto for the such purpose shall not be permitted if these are sensitive personal data, excluding the case when the insurance undertaking requires sensitive personal data in the case provided for in subsection 218 (2) of this Act.

 (2) An insurance undertaking shall be entitled to transmit to its reinsurance undertaking without the consent of the data subject personal data related to the insured event for determining the obligation to perform a reinsurance contract and the scope thereof. The transmission of personal data to the reinsurance undertaking or granting access thereto for the such purpose shall not be permitted if these are sensitive personal data, excluding the case provided for in subsection 218 (2) of this Act.

*Analysis:* The insurance company seems to have cited a valid legal basis to allow them access to the data of the third party. The scope should be narrowed only to the subject that is the subject of the request. There should not be an error in the identity of the rider.

*BH:* [https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/513700339|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/513700339]

*Analysis that it's 7 years in Estonian and confirmation by the tax team* 

See analysis below



*Proposed solution:*

# *Option 1 (desirable).* This option addresses the current non-documented internally and document externally in Privacy Notices position of Bolt to keep tax data for up to 10 years. This response can potentially get the Eater to file a complaint with AKI as he would not agree on such an extensive retention period. 
## This response explains to the Eater that while the Accounting Act in Estonia prescribes 7 years, GDPR allows to keep data if this is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defend of legal claims. Given Bolt’s cross-border operations and potential tax audits in these countries, Bolt retains the invoices for up to 10 years. The response is drafted below

[https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ylGciZS_EIQ_ehDJanTYx3-IAajyS55wnkuAH2rwJdY/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1ylGciZS_EIQ_ehDJanTYx3-IAajyS55wnkuAH2rwJdY/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 

# *Option 2.* This option proposes to state that in Estonia we keep the data for 7 years. Given that Bolt’s retention stance is not documented yet, this can calm down the user from filing a claim. However, if the Eater further will assess the retention statement against privacy notices updates or other responses from Bolt, Eater can file a complaint that Bolt leverages deceptive practices and does not provide full transparency or real information to users. While this option is a good short-term solution, it can have significant implications in the future.

*Meeting notes* {{2025-02-18}} *:* 

* We have asked Lofandi multiple times but they keep telling us they can’t fit components which could sustain higher voltage.
* The Lofandi hub cannot turn off itself.
* We need to keep the hublock powered as we need wheeltick information. 
* Mitigation options:
** :yellow_circle:  Redesign to the controller schematics which would limit surge voltages.
*** Would result in delay and might be risky.
** :red_cross: External box which would sustain the surge voltages
*** We would not want an external box as it would enable opening the hublock by external power source.
** (x) In-line component inside the cable - this is a long-term solution which would need more development. 
** :red_cross: Powering the wheeltick from 24V line - with this we would have a risk that if the lock is not functional, the IoT is also down, there’s also a risk that the hublock could damage the IoT.
** :red_cross: Rear hublock - adds 1kg mass and requires UART, does not fit in width.
** :red_cross: Using light’s output

# If you have some service provider who can document the actual state of the vehicles, that would be good. If not, then we should do it ourselves. This includes taking photos of the vehicles, defects, paint scratches etc. If this comes to a dispute, the more documents/evidence we have, the better.

            parameters = parameters.replace('""', '"')

            if parameters[0] == '"':

            parameters = json.loads(parameters)

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 27 January 2025, UK [rider|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/78744166/overview] (Johan Amos) [wrote|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/512547784] to Bolt CS to flag account compromise.
** Rider noticed rides being taken by someone else on their account. In particular, they claim their phone was stolen and used to take Bolt trips.
** Rider flagged that their credit card company was already looking into suspicious charges - they just wanted to know how to log out of Bolt from all devices. 
** On the same day (27 Jan), CS confirmed to the rider that all devices had been logged out of their account.
* On the same day, rider requested “_details of the fraudulent rides_”. This counts as a DSAR.
** Rides were: “_£35.40 26/01/25… £6.00 26/01/25_”. CS has not responded on this point.
** Rider also asked “_Can you tell where my account is logged in?_” CS responded “_At the moment the only logged-in session is with the device you are using. Any other device has been deactivated_”. As such, this element has been addressed.
* Having reviewed their account, relevant details are as follows:
** Account is currently active. Does not look like it was ever blocked.
** Only one device is now active on the rider’s account. All other devices were deactivated on 27 Jan.
** Trips at issue are as follows:
*** [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/555905821/25?orderTryId=1127019395|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/555905821/25?orderTryId=1127019395]
**** Final trip price: £35.40
**** Pickup: 97 Shroffold Road, Bromley BR1 5PD
**** Destination: 6-17 Tottenham Court Road, London W1T 1AZ
**** Status: Finished
*** [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/555889603/25?orderTryId=1126963987|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/555889603/25?orderTryId=1126963987]
**** Pickup: 118-132 New Oxford Street, London WC1A 1HL
**** Destination: Archway Station, JUNCTION ROAD, London
**** Status: Cancelled (Client did not show - hence £6.00 cancellation fee)
*** No other trips taken on 26 Jan incurred any cost. 
* This SD ticket was raised on 31 January. Unfortunately, insufficient information until 18 February (a considerable delay).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Nothing to suggest explicitly that the rider is pursuing a claim. As such, this can be handled by Privacy.
* This counts as a personal data breach, as temporary unauthorised access to a rider’s Bolt account (c. 24 hours in total).
** Date of awareness of Privacy Team was 18 February 2025.
** ODPO Team notified [here|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C0678KJ49UH/p1739903105850949].
** IMO, unlikely to be reportable, however awaiting ODPO conclusion.
* There is also a DSAR element to deal with, which we need to action by 27 February.
** Trips details extracted [here|https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1LohtMJQ4eU6RCGtNsTf4mo3n16b3VEMe]. I have redacted _precise_ addresses (leaving just postcode, as we have done for similar requests in the past where the account is compromised), as well as driver info.
** Also, registered on Cognito ([Link|https://www.cognitoforms.com/bolttechnologyo%C3%BC/datasubjectrightsrequeststracker/entries/1-all-entries/1121]).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Await ODPO confirmation re whether this is reportable (IMO this is unlikely).
* To address the DSAR element, provide the rider with the requested data in advance of 27 Feb.

I went to mylab today to discuss the brake test method. Here are some comments about the test.

*Brake wear test:*

25km/h, 5000 brakes, compare the brake stop distance at 0 and 5000 cycles, and compare the brake pad thickness before and after the test. Push lever force 100N, Brake frequency 30 times per minute.

*Brake performance:*

The expansion brake cannot be completely locked, so this test has no reference value for the expansion brake.
The drum brake, disc brake, and V-brake can all lock completely. Currently, the laboratory cannot test how much force is required to rotate the tire after it locks up. I also wanted to fix the tire and use a pull machine to press the front fork, but this may cause damage to the rim and brake, and the accuracy of the test results cannot be guaranteed. 
But the lab proposed another method, applying a force of 180N on the brake lever and testing the braking distance to compare the braking performance. [~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] How do you think?

* *Basic* – The maximum vehicle age is 30 years. Vehicles from 1995 and newer are eligible.

Hey everyone, 

Regarding the fraud questions, 

The fraud check is automated, there is no manual human review, because it is a profiling query that runs once a day and compares conditions. 

What it does, and maybe this is a suggestion for education of drivers further on and maybe change in description when applying such campaigns, is that the check does not deduct bonus, but it flags orders that campaigns should not count towards validation of achieved goal. It is a condition check, so technically drivers did less valid transactions than needed, valid being a word that might need to be added to next iterations. 

As for the conditions, the profiling compares driver volumes prior and within the timeframe of enrollment for a campaign and also checks any other suspicious conditions, like short rides, fast durations and odd distances within that period and comparing them to the driver’s average. 
As we also mentioned in the previous ticket, there was a technical issue with the profiling that was maybe too aggressive in the flagging back then, a thing that is now solved. 

Let me know if more info is needed,

Hi [~accountid:5b7beb0cc4e4892a5b7889d6],

Here is the inital guidance for ease of reference:

*Initial Guidance*

*Initial thoughts based on ticket and RFC*: We should notify users that responses are aided by translation tools and limit the use of machine translation to low risk CS interactions.
*Limit DeepL use to low-risk, routine CS interactions and notify users of machine translation tool use.* High-risk cases (e.g., safety-related tickets, high-value claims, privacy complaints or worker classification issues) should be escalated to native-speaking staff (e.g. local ops) and/or legal in line with existing escalation processes. I’d also recommend notifying users when responses are aided by translation tools to maintain transparency and meet local consumer law obligations in all markets; unless doing so significantly impacts user experience.
h3. Specific Challenges and Mitigations:
# *Complex Legal Terminology:*
*Problem:* Different EU countries, and countries outside the EU where Bolt operates, have distinct legal terminologies and frameworks. A term used in one country may not have a direct legal counterpart in another, which could create discrepancies communications with users. DeepL may misinterpret terms that have legal consequences, leading to inaccuracies or unintended assumption of liability by Bolt.
*Mitigation:* Use DeepL for routine inquiries only. High-risk interactions should be escalated to native speakers in local ops or legal. Notifying users that translation tools are used may also mitigate the risk in the event mistakes are made in early CS interactions.
# *Cultural Differences:*
*Problem:* Machine translations can miss cultural nuances, leading to potential miscommunication.
*Mitigation:* Routine inquiries can be handled by DeepL; sensitive cases must be escalated. Inform users about translation tool usage unless it significantly detracts from the UX. As suggested in the RFC, thoroughly testing the language models prior to implementation and periodic checks by native speakers will also help mitigate this risk.
# *Confidentiality, User Privacy and Ethical Considerations:*
*Problem:* Machine translation could expose sensitive user data.
*Mitigation:* High-risk cases involving sensitive data should use manual translation and sensitive/identifiable user data should not be entered into translation tools where possible. Ensure DeepL’s strictest privacy settings are enabled for routine cases. Suggest privacy review (cc: [~accountid:712020:0c8dd65b-46d5-4dc0-b5bd-76209c1e8048]) to ensure DPAs and relevant EU/National privacy risks adequately mapped and mitigated.

These same risks apply and must be acknowledged, HOWEVER:

* In light of the positive results from the low risk application and the mistakes attributable to native language lacking the MM specific expertise, there is an argument that utilising machine learning tools to ensure the most competent team member handles a MM safety case might outweigh the risks outlined above.
* Ultimately this is a judgement call, considering which approach balances costs, legal exposure and importantly, the best outcomes for Bolt and affected users. *There are no obvious legal blockers, save those outlined above, to adopting this new approach.*
* I’d still recommend notifying users that interactions and responses are aided by machine translation and for high risk issues to be escalated to the relevant field counsel  in line with existing escalation processes. 

Hope this helps and as always, available to jump on a call to discuss the issue further.

Thanks for the review!

The thing is, that we’ve shortened the amount of info we’re requesting for “regular” NDAs (= non-onsites, just intro meeting with a recruiter about confidential roles we don’t want to be wildly known that we’re hiring for, aka new countries lanches etc.).

The info requested through Spotdraft template has been reduced to contact details (phone & email address), so no ID number: [https://app.spotdraft.com/editor-v3/templates/9701/new|https://app.spotdraft.com/editor-v3/templates/9701/new|smart-link]

*Intelligent Recommendations and Defaulting* for Expense Items uses the following information from the scanned receipts and expense submitter for Expense Item predictions:

* Merchant Name
* Currency Code
* Receipt Amount
* Receipt Date
* Expense Payee

For the combination of input fields, Workday recommends up to 5 most likely Expense Items. In scenarios where the Machine Learning (ML) model is +confident+, the value of the field is defaulted with the top Expense Item recommendation.

Intelligent Recommendations and Defaulting for Expense Items uses tenant-specific models that are trained on customer contributed data. The customer contributed data might include historical data of expense report lines that are approved and created from an OCR scanned receipt. 

Recommendations won’t be shown in Workday with poor prediction accuracy.

 

Also, the scanning takes a bit of time. I downloaded these receipts from random ERs submitted in WD and added the receipts via receipt scanning and came back a minute later. That was what I saw:

 

!IMG_0202.PNG|width=50%,alt="IMG_0202.PNG"!

 

!IMG_0201.PNG|width=50%,alt="IMG_0201.PNG"!

If I go to the desktop version I can also see these recommended expense items:

 

!image-20250129-104441.png|width=50%,alt="image-20250129-104441.png"!

 

!image-20250129-104507.png|width=50%,alt="image-20250129-104507.png"!

In cases where WD will not suggest any items, it may be because the OCR can’t read the receipt well or it is not confident to suggest any expense items.

Workday recommends keeping these receipts and taking screenshots so we can create a case to them.

I recommend scanning the receipts (either taking the picture or adding it via photos) right away when the cost has been incurred and just leaving them there and submitting an expense report later either via desktop or mobile.

It takes time for the OCR to scan the receipt, and the recommendations also appear on the desktop, not only on the mobile

*Overall Impression:*

The provided DPA is reasonably comprehensive, covering many essential aspects of data protection law. However, several areas present potential risks for Bolt and require careful consideration and possible revision. The DPA seems heavily weighted towards protecting Mastercard, so certain clauses need adjustments to better balance the obligations and liabilities between the parties.

*Identified Risks and Recommended Changes:*

# *Risk:* Broad definition of "Business Purpose" (Section 1). :green_circle: *Low risk*
#* The definitions of "Mastercard Purposes" and "Customer Purposes" are quite broad. This lack of specificity could lead to disputes about the scope of permissible data processing. For instance, "data analysis" and "benchmarking" by Mastercard, while potentially legitimate, could encompass activities that Bolt might find objectionable or non-compliant with its own privacy policies.
# *Risk:* Unilateral right to suspend services (Section 5). :green_circle: *Low risk*
#* Mastercard reserves the right to immediately suspend services if Bolt breaches the agreement. This is a harsh penalty and could severely disrupt Bolt's operations. The clause lacks any provision for Bolt to rectify the breach or appeal the suspension.
# *Risk:* Transfer of Data outside country of collection (Section 5). :yellow_circle: *Medium risk*
#* The clause regarding data transfer and storage outside the collection country places a significant burden on Bolt. Bolt must ensure it has all necessary consents and authorizations for such transfers. This could be difficult to manage for a large, international customer base. The language needs to be tightened.
# *Risk:* Notification Obligations (Section 6). :green_circle: *Low risk re timeline /* :yellow_circle: *Medium risk re prior written authorization* 
#* The notification timeline (48 hours) for any data breach-related requests or investigations could be challenging to meet in all situations. This timeframe might be too short, especially for complex or large-scale incidents. Also, the requirement to respond to such requests only with Mastercard's prior written authorization could hinder Bolt's ability to respond promptly and effectively.
# *Risk:* Personal Data Breach Notification (Section 8). :green_circle: *Low*
#* While the breach notification clause is fairly detailed, it heavily emphasizes Mastercard's role and notification to Mastercard. It could be clarified that the customer also has obligations.
# *Risk:* Liability (Section 9). :yellow_circle: *Medium - will suggest to rephrase liability*
#* The liability clause states that each party is liable for damages resulting from a violation of privacy law. However, it also mentions that Mastercard can claim back compensation from Bolt for Bolt’s "part of responsibility". This could lead to complex disputes over apportioning liability.
# *Risk:* Audit Clause (Annex 2).:green_circle: *Low - no changes will be suggested*
#* The audit clause in Annex 2 allows each party to audit the other. While this is important, the clause could be more detailed about the scope, frequency, and procedure for audits.
# *Risk:* Governing Law and Jurisdiction (Section 10 and Annex 2). (?) *it’s unclear - the governing law is the law of the principal agreement. Do we have a principal agreement?*
#* The governing law and jurisdiction clauses could be unfavorable to Bolt, depending on its location and legal resources. The specific governing law and jurisdiction should be carefully considered.



These considerations/risks will be addressed directly in the agreement, if required.

{quote}Unless the failed orders that we pay for (failed after preparation) do not follow the same pattern as compensations.{quote}

Once more,  we charge commission on *realized orders*. Even if an order fails after preparation or during courier pickup, we *still collect the commission* and we still add it as a normal sale on their balance.

The Customer Payments Operations Team does not have the required tools/permissions to issue refunds. If you are not able to issue the refund then we kindly ask you to check with your Team Lead on how to solve this case. You may need to request the following accesses in Admin to be able to issue refund for orders if you previously do not have such:

* *Bolt+*: subscription_offer_customer_support



{color:#bf2600}*Note: A failed card payment can’t be refunded to the card. Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.*{color}

For issues with refunds from Beehive, kindly reach out to #beehive-agent-support on Slack.

It is true that in the past Customer Payments Operations could make refunds but we are currently changing our processes as manual refunds via Customer Payments is not the same as refunds via CS/Beehive. Doing manual refunds of payments on our end leads to system data inconsistency and while it is possible to do it for exceptional cases (incidents), it would be really much better to use the existing features of refunds. With the accesses I shared previously, I believe it should be possible to refunds these orders without further assistance from Commerce Customer Payments.

{color:#ff5630}For older orders refund, kindly check with your team lead as they have the required accesses to perform such operations.{color}

*Test results:*

When water is in the battery main connector and driving is allowed from IoT side, then scooter behaves normally. Riding is safe and comfortable. 



Considering other possible short circuits that can happen in the connector:

# Charging pin and P+

This is right now the reason why scooter doesn’t ride. IoT is disabling the throttle if voltage is detected on the charging pin. If charger check logic is removed then riding would be possible. Additionally, the scooter would also have an informational error, which will help us understand the scope of the problem. 

# GND and ID pin

If short is between ID pin and GND then it’s similar to ID pin being pulled down by resistor in the ECU. This doesn’t cause problems. 

# CAN H and CAN L

If a short is between CAN H and CAN L then depending on the resistance of the water CAN communication could be interrupted. Resistance of water is hard to predict, it depends largely on the ion content of the water. CAN communication problems can be monitored when IoT has implemented error for checking water in main connector. 



*Conclusion:* From scooter side, we can continue with making the charger check configurable. And implement an informational error for water in main connector. These changes will be implemented in the next IoT release.

Hi [~accountid:6231c75b8c349300687c581e],

From a legal perspective, its important that we answer the following questions when selecting a suitable charity partner:

* Does the organisation hold a non-profit status?
* Is the organisation listed in the register of NGOs allowing tax benefits?
* What is the mission of the organisation, does it align or share similarities to our own?
* What are the short- and long-term goals of the organisation?
* How will the organisation use our donation (please include allocation between administrative costs and funds given directly to the cause)?
* What documents there will be to demonstrate the use of our donation?
* How does the organisation communicate its mission and progress to donors?
* How does the organisation ensure that the beneficiaries have a say in the decision-making process?

Only once we have satisfactory responses to this list of questions can we be confident that the partner is one that we can support.

That being said, I’ve reviewed the agreement and haven’t identified any red flags. I’ve only added the option for either party to terminate the agreement for convenience.

Hi all - I have reviewed this from a Privacy POV and my thoughts are as follows:

* FIFO queues are generally not as high risk for us, as they are limited in geographic scope (i.e., airports). However, as we are all aware, we are getting some heat in the UK about how it is not always fully clear to drivers how work is being allocated to them, and so any new features that we roll out in this context (particularly where the processes are fully automated, as they naturally are here) have a heightened risk profile. Similar to Anusha, I would say that this feature is at least {color:#ff991f}*moderate risk*{color}, but surrounding factors cumulatively elevate the risk to {color:#bf2600}*high*{color}.
* The main concern with this feature from a Privacy POV is with *transparency*. In light of the heat we are currently getting in the UK, we need to aim to de-risk this feature by ensuring we are being transparent *_enough_* about how this work re work allocation without revealing confidential information about our algorithms.
* I understand from the [feature document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1yWAQEj2FS_TBKZbe2NN5PmttLptKgDwzz7d3erp8JAo/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.8oa2657wwtlp] that a UI integration is being considered to communicate to drivers “_you’ve been put in last position because you’ve canceled X orders in a row_”. This would help to de-risk the feature by providing additional transparency. We can also consider updates the Privacy Notice from our side.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Conclusion:*

From a strictly Privacy POV, we can green-light this feature *_provided that_* we include a UI integration that explains the FIFO logic (at a high level) to impacted drivers that are bumped to the back of the queue.

It is open to the business to proceed with the feature without doing the above, but this exposes us to similar risks that we have already flagged about the ICO investigation.
{panel}
